sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To evaluate the safety and efficacy of CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy in a patient with refractory lupus nephritis who experienced severe disease flare during immunosuppressive washout, and to assess whether pulse corticosteroid intervention affects CAR T cell therapeutic outcomes.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We report a single case of a 22-year-old woman with SLE and lupus podocytopathy refractory to multiple therapies including rituximab, belimumab and obinutuzumab. The patient was treated under single-patient IND (#30146) with autologous CD19 CAR T cells (KYV-101). During the preinfusion washout period, she developed severe lupus flare requiring pulse intravenous methylprednisolone. Clinical outcomes, CAR T cell expansion, B cell depletion and laboratory parameters were monitored before and after therapy.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Despite experiencing severe lupus flare (fever, rash, arthritis, anti-dsDNA elevation, hypocomplementaemia) during washout, pulse methylprednisolone (250 mg intravenous, rapidly tapered) successfully controlled symptoms without compromising subsequent CAR T cell expansion (peak 15.5 cells/µL on day 7). The patient achieved sustained clinical remission with SLE Disease Activity Index Score decreasing from 17 prior to leukapheresis to 4 by week 17. At 12 months postinfusion, she remained in drug-free remission with stable kidney function and had returned to full-time work.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This case report illustrates that targeted pulse corticosteroids during CAR T cell therapy washout can effectively manage severe lupus flares without impairing therapeutic efficacy.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has emerged as a promising treatment for refractory autoimmune diseases like SLE but requires immunosuppressive washout periods that create risk for severe disease flares.

The management of autoimmune flares during CAR T cell therapy preparation remains challenging, as intensified immunosuppression may potentially compromise CAR T cell expansion and therapeutic efficacy.

This case illustrates that targeted pulse corticosteroids during immunosuppressive washout allow control of severe lupus flares without impairing subsequent CAR T cell therapeutic efficacy, as evidenced by successful CAR T cell expansion and sustained drug-free remission at 12 months postinfusion.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: These findings provide clinicians with a practical bridging strategy to safely manage severe autoimmune flares during CAR T cell therapy preparation, potentially expanding access to this transformative treatment for patients with highly active SLE.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: SLE remains a challenging autoimmune condition, particularly when complicated by lupus nephritis, which affects up to 65% of patients and contributes significantly to morbidity and mortality.1 While corticosteroids and immunosuppressive medications are the mainstay of SLE treatment,2 genetically engineered chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells, designed to target CD19 B cell surface antigen, have emerged as a highly effective treatment for refractory SLE.3 4 For autologous CAR T cell therapy in SLE,3 5 immunosuppressive medications are usually discontinued 1–2 weeks prior to apheresis collection. Current European Society for Blood and Marrow Transplantation-International Society for Cellular Therapy (EBMT-ISCT) and Joint Accreditation Committee of ISCT and EBMT (JACIE) expert recommendations specify that steroids may be administered at ≤10 mg/day prednisone equivalent before leukapheresis, though higher doses are permitted as bridging therapy between leukapheresis and lymphodepletion if clinically needed.5 According to these guidelines, immunosuppression can be resumed during the CAR T cell manufacturing process, but must be withdrawn 1–2 weeks prior to the lymphodepleting regimen in advance of CAR T cell infusion.3 5 These periods of immunosuppressive treatment interruption, while short, introduce an increased risk for SLE disease activity, namely flare.6 This risk may be compounded by the fact that current CAR T cell clinical trials enrol patients with active and refractory disease. Any flare would necessitate intensification of immunosuppression,7 with the potential risk of dampening CAR T cell expansion and/or function.8 Here, we report a case of a patient with lupus nephritis with active and refractory disease, which flared during the treatment washout period. Despite this, she achieved sustained drug-free remission after CD19-CAR T cell therapy.

sec.title: Patients and methods
sec.p: The patient was initially diagnosed with SLE, in late 2017 at the age of 22 years, with renal involvement. She underwent a kidney biopsy first in October 2018, which revealed class II mesangial lupus nephritis with superimposed podocytopathy. She experienced a relapsing-remitting nephrotic syndrome course beginning in 2018. She had an initial response with steroids and mycophenolate mofetil that led to initial remission, but frequent relapses followed, requiring tacrolimus and being maintained in remission with rituximab. While off rituximab, she experienced a relapse that was refractory to belimumab, obinutuzumab and was maintained in partial response with tacrolimus. Although serum creatinine remained within the normal range, the second renal biopsy in June 2022 demonstrated class II mesangial lupus nephritis with podocytopathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS), mild tubulointerstitial nephritis and moderate-to-severe interstitial fibrosis involving 50% of the biopsied tissue, indicating permanent renal damage. Despite treatment with various agents, she experienced recurrent flares of SLE, as well manifested by rash, arthritis and fatigue, along with persistent nephrotic range proteinuria and hypocomplementaemia. The patient’s nephrotic syndrome did not achieve complete remission, except during the period of rituximab therapy, supporting the notion that the disease is B cell-mediated. Following her relapse, treatment with obinutuzumab effectively depleted circulating B cells; however, this was not associated with a corresponding clinical response (online supplemental table 1). The lack of response to these conventional treatments, combined with the presence of an FSGS variant—both indicators of poor prognosis and increased risk of progressive renal failure9—led us to hypothesise that the patient may benefit from more intensive B cell-targeted therapy using CAR T cells directed against CD19.

She was therefore referred to the UMass Chan Rheumatology clinic for consideration of CD19-CAR T cell therapy. She was consented under a single patient IND (#30146). Tacrolimus (2 mg every 12 hours) and mycophenolate mofetil (1000 mg every 12 hours) were discontinued 7 days prior to leukapheresis; she continued on prednisone at 10 mg/day. Following leukapheresis on 17 January 2024, tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil were immediately resumed. Immunosuppressive medications were stopped again 9 days prior to the planned infusion date on 20 March 2024 (day 0), except for 10 mg/day of prednisone. Two days later and prior to initiation of the lymphodepleting conditioning regimen, she experienced an acute SLE flare manifested by fever (39°C), fatigue, rash, arthritis, oral ulcers, otalgia and dizziness. Laboratory tests were consistent with an SLE flare, with increased anti-dsDNA antibodies, severe hypocomplementaemia (both C3 and C4), anaemia and leucopenia. Given the flare severity, in consultation with the sponsor and with the Federal Drug Administration (FDA), it was decided to initiate treatment with pulse intravenous methylprednisolone (250 mg on day −7), quickly tapered to 100 mg on day −6, 50 mg on days −5 and −4, followed by 10 mg on day −3. The patient had a rapid response to the initial bolus with substantial clinical improvement, although her laboratory markers of lupus activity, including high titre of anti-dsDNA antibodies and low levels of complement, persisted. This rapid clinical improvement allowed the prompt corticosteroid taper, undertaken to minimise further immunosuppression during the lymphodepletion regimen and to reduce any detrimental effects of corticosteroids on CAR T cell function and expansion.8

Following her improvement, lymphodepletion was started as planned, consisting of fludarabine (30 mg/m2/day) and cyclophosphamide (300 mg/m2/day) on days −5 through −3, followed by a single infusion of 1×108 anti-CD19 CAR T lymphocytes with a CD28-based construct (KYV-101, Kyverna Therapeutics) on day 0. Her prior core immunosuppressive regimen (tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil) was not resumed after KYV-101 infusion. The complete medication regimen before, during and after CAR T cell therapy is summarised in figure 1.

caption.title: Timeline of immunosuppressive therapy and medication management relative to chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell infusion. The administration schedule of medications before and after CAR T cell infusion (day 0). Mycophenolate mofetil and tacrolimus were administered until day −10. Pulse steroids (methylprednisolone) were administered from days −7 to −3 to treat the lupus flare that occurred after discontinuation of immunosuppressive medications. Lymphodepletion regimen included cyclophosphamide and fludarabine from days −5 to −3. Following CAR T cell infusion, tocilizumab was administered at days 1 and 5–7 to manage cytokine release syndrome (CRS), and dexamethasone was initiated on day 5 and continued through day 14 and beyond to treat residual symptoms. The dose of each medication is written in mg. On day 0, the patient’s weight and height were 47.6 kg and 1.67 m, respectively.

sec.p: The patient experienced grade 1 cytokine release syndrome (fever up to 38.7°C) for 8 days after CAR T cell infusion for which she received tocilizumab infusions (8 mg/kg) on days 1, 5, 6 and 7. As the fever persisted, she also developed bilateral scleritis in the absence of a documented infectious source. Intravenous dexamethasone 4 mg every 8 hours and steroid eye drops were initiated, after which fever and scleritis resolved. The patient was discharged on day 14, while being tapered on dexamethasone (oral, 2 mg/day on discharge). On day 28, dexamethasone was switched to 10 mg/day prednisone. As the patient subsequently experienced bilateral knee and left ankle pain (day 33), the dose of prednisone was increased to 20 mg/day. On another attempt to titrate prednisone (17.5 mg/day), she developed bilateral scleritis (day 41), which resolved on increasing prednisone back to 20 mg/day together with prednisolone eye drops.

On day 90, her prednisone dose was tapered to 17.5 mg/day and further tapered off over the following 60 days without incident. At 6 months postinfusion, the patient had successfully discontinued all immunosuppressive medications, including steroids, and had returned to full-time work.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: CAR T cells expanded as anticipated, with a peak on day 7 (15.5 cells/uL) and were detectable in blood (≥ 1 cell/uL) until day 90. B cells were undetectable in peripheral blood and remained so through the 6-month follow-up.

By week 8, lupus-specific laboratory values significantly improved (figure 2). Anti-dsDNA antibodies, which peaked at approximately 2000 IU/mL during the washout period, declined to <50 IU/mL by week 8 and continued to decrease through 6 months. Anti-Sm antibodies, another highly specific SLE biomarker, decreased from approximately 8 IU/mL to undetectable levels by week 5 following the infusion.

caption.title: Serial measurements of disease activity and key laboratory parameters before and after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell infusion. Longitudinal changes in disease activity and laboratory values from 10 weeks before to 25 weeks after CAR T cell infusion (week 0). Parameters include anti-dsDNA antibodies, Sm antibody, complement components (C3, C4), white blood cells (WBC), haemoglobin, platelets, IgG serum levels, serum creatinine, serum albumin, protein-to-creatinine ratio and SLE Disease Activity Index (SLEDAI). The preinfusion period (−10 to 0 weeks) captures the flare during the immunosuppressive washout phase, during which anti-dsDNA antibodies peaked at approximately 2000 IU/mL and complement levels reached nadirs (C3~30 mg/dL, C4<5 mg/dL). The immediate postlymphodepletion period shows expected cytopenias, with WBC dropping to ~1×10³/μL and haemoglobin to ~8 g/dL, both recovering by week 5. The timeline demonstrates robust immunological response following CAR T cell therapy: anti-dsDNA antibodies decreased continuously; anti-Sm antibodies became undetectable by week 5; complement C3 and C4 normalised by week 10. Notably, IgG levels stabilised at about 500 mg/dL post-treatment; protein-to-creatinine ratio decreased from peak levels of ~8000 mg/g to 2000–3000 mg/g by week 10, with residual proteinuria likely representing irreversible renal damage; serum albumin correspondingly improved from ~2.5 g/dL to ~4 g/dL. Overall, the SLEDAI Score improved from 17 (preleukapheresis) to 4 by week 20, reflecting clinical remission. Red data points indicate values that were below laboratory detection levels. Horizontal dotted lines serve different purposes across graphs: in WBC, platelets and albumin graphs, they represent normal range boundaries; in anti-dsDNA and Sm antibody graphs, they indicate positive thresholds; in haemoglobin, complement component (C3, C4) and serum IgG graphs, they represent lower limits of normal; and in the protein-to-creatinine ratio graph, the line represents the upper limit of normal.

sec.p: Complement levels demonstrated marked recovery; C3 increased from a nadir of approximately 30 mg/dL during the washout period to normal levels (>83 mg/dL) by week 8, and C4 rose from <5 mg/dL to within the normal range (>15 mg/dL) over the same timeframe.

Haematological indices also improved following treatment. White cell count, which had dropped to approximately 1×10³/μL following chemotherapy and CAR T cell infusion, recovered to normal levels (3.8–10.8×10³/μL) by week 3. Similarly, haemoglobin levels increased from approximately 8 g/dL to levels above 11 g/dL by week 3. Platelet counts fluctuated between 200×10³/μL and 500×10³/μL, occasionally exceeding the upper normal limit.

Proteinuria decreased from peak levels of approximately 8000 mg/g creatinine to 2000–3000 mg/g creatinine by week 8, indicating partial improvement. IgG levels, initially elevated dramatically during the washout period (>1300 mg/dL), gradually decreased following treatment and remained stable, although below the normal range (<600 mg/dL).

The SLE Disease Activity Index Score decreased from 17 prior to leukapheresis to 4 by week 17 postinfusion and remained stable through month 12. Sustained clinical disease remission was noted at the 1 year postinfusion visit. Kidney function remained stable throughout (serum creatinine level at 0.58 mg/dL; eGFR >90 mL/min/1.732) further documenting the substantial clinical improvement.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This case demonstrates that pulse corticosteroids during immunosuppression washout prior to CAR T cell infusion can effectively control severe lupus flares without compromising therapeutic efficacy. The successful CAR T cell expansion (peak 15.5 cells/μL) despite pulse methylprednisolone administration challenges concerns about corticosteroid interference with cellular therapy outcomes.8 10 The brief duration of exposure (5 days) and timing prior to lymphodepletion likely allowed clearance of immunosuppressive effects before the critical expansion phase.

The pharmacokinetics of mycophenolate mofetil merit consideration. With a half-life of 9–17 hours for its active metabolite, mycophenolate mofetil would clear within a few days of discontinuation.11 The severe flare occurred shortly after the second mycophenolate mofetil discontinuation, when therapeutic levels would have rapidly declined, highlighting the vulnerability of patients with active disease during washout periods.

During the postinfusion period, we observed limited clinical manifestations on tapering steroids. It is unclear whether these manifestations represented disease-related inflammatory activity or, as recently reported, local immune effector cell-associated toxicity syndrome (LICATS), a specific type of CD19 CAR T toxicity in patients with systemic autoimmune disease.12 LICATS is most likely driven by local B cell clearance and transient inflammatory processes, distinguished from true flares by its timing, lack of serological activity and self-limited course that usually resolves spontaneously or with short glucocorticosteroid treatment.12 Our patient’s scleritis and arthralgia during steroid taper may represent LICATS.

Importantly, despite residual nephrotic range proteinuria, IgG levels remained ≥500 mg/dL and no intravenous immunoglobulins (IVIG) administration was required. The residual nephrotic-range proteinuria (protein/Cr ratio of 2779 mg/g and 3274 mg/g at 6 months and 12 months post CAR-T treatment, respectively) likely reflects irreversible renal damage, consistent with the biopsy-documented moderate–severe interstitial fibrosis and FSGS. This is further supported by the concurrent normalisation of biomarkers, including anti-dsDNA antibodies, serum albumin and complement levels demonstrating a lack of ongoing active lupus nephritis and indicating maximal therapeutic response in light of the pre-existing renal injury (figure 2).

It is intriguing that another case of podocytopathy has been reported in the context of CAR T therapy in SLE. Mackensen and colleagues, in their initial series, described a patient with lupus who developed podocytopathy 4 months after CAR T infusion, which resolved promptly with a pulse of glucocorticoids.13 Despite the commonality of podocytopathy, that case differed substantially: there was no prior history of podocytopathy and it was not associated with systemic lupus activation, in stark contrast to our patient, who had refractory systemic lupus with chronic renal involvement.

In conclusion, this case documents the clinical impact after a single infusion of CD19-CAR T cells in a poor prognosis case of lupus nephritis refractory to other therapeutic modalities, including prior B cell targeting agents. It also highlights the risk that patients with active disease may experience flares when their existing treatment is washed out to enable CAR T cell infusion. In our case, the implementation of pulse intravenous steroids controlled the lupus flare, enabling the patient to proceed with CAR T cell infusion. Her favourable clinical outcome with this approach suggests that the pulse steroids did not compromise CAR T cell efficacy and raises the question of whether to pre-emptively bridge with high-dose steroids, to avoid disease flares.
